result.white_space:
1) The software layer is not white space. At least 8 Nigerian vendors sell ledger, loan and member-portal SaaS to cooperatives at N50-100k/month. Coopra targets staff cooperatives with deduction tracking. ProbityCoop claims automated dues reconciliation. SmartTeller has an AI loan evaluator. Collectiva is pitching OCR and open banking. 'Digitise books, member statements, digital guarantors' is table stakes.

2) What I found no direct competitor doing:
(a) WhatsApp-first member and treasurer interface. Cooperativ references WhatsApp only as the problem it replaces. I found no evidence of a WhatsApp-native product, but I could not verify every vendor's roadmap.
(b) AI-vision migration of handwritten exercise books from phone photos as a day-one onboarding wedge. Collectiva mentions OCR only for statements and receipts, not handwritten ledgers.
(c) Reconciliation of employer check-off remittances against the deduction schedule, to detect short or missing months. Vendors say 'deduction tracking' and 'reduce manual reconciliation', but I found no product built around employer-side reconciliation and dispute evidence. This is the strongest software-level differentiator, and it is defensible only if paired with employer relationships or payroll-file ingestion.
(d) An inter-cooperative surplus-to-deficit wholesale or treasury market. I found none of the software vendors offering it, and no player doing it in the software layer. Only CREDICORP-style government wholesale lines exist, on the funding side.

3) Layer (d) is the only place with real white space, but it is a different business. It is a credit, treasury and regulatory business and needs an MFB or bank partner. The legality and licensing of cooperative-to-cooperative lending under the Cooperative Societies Act and CBN rules is unverified here. It also depends on the software wedge reaching enough cooperatives with clean ledgers, and Asusu's apparent fade shows how hard that is.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Partial. The strongest evidence is that vendors sell and price this software:
- SmartTeller lists N50k-100k/month plans and claims 1,056 registered cooperatives (https://smartteller.tech/cooperative). This is self-reported but validates the price band.
- Cooperativ claims 500+ cooperatives (https://www.getcooperativ.com/).
- ProbityCoop lists SterlingBank Staff Cooperative and Irorun MPCS as clients (https://probitysoftware.com/coop.html).
- THRiFTy lists NASUCOOP and OGTV Staff Cooperatives, with a user quote about removing 'back-breaking stress' from ledger updates (https://thriftycoop.com/en/).
- Asusu reportedly served about 100 cooperatives and about $2.5M in savings and credit around 2019, per a search-result summary (https://techcabal.com/2019/08/09/meet-asusu-the-startup-digitising-informal-savings-and-credit-associations-in-northern-nigeria/).
- The federal government created CREDICORP in April 2024 to wholesale-finance cooperatives and others lending to salary earners; about 1.6M applications came in by May 2024 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerian_Consumer_Credit_Corporation).
- Salary-loan repayment by payroll deduction (IPPIS) is confirmed as the norm for bank and MFB loans (https://www.creditdirect.ng/blog/payday-loans-nigeria), which supports the check-off underwriting logic.

NOT verified, because the WebSearch budget ran out at 200 calls mid-task and several pages returned 403 or 404:
- The '~10% flat per year' cooperative rate.
- Idle cooperative surplus earning 3-8% while other societies ration loans.
- Embezzlement or unreconciled-remittance collapses.
- Any demand signal specifically for inter-cooperative lending.
- Any funded startup in this niche.
Absence of funding among direct competitors is itself a warning that ARPU or willingness to pay may be low.
result.kill_reason: n/a. The idea is not killed because no strong incumbent dominates and no funded leader was found. The software wedge as pitched is crowded and commoditised. The idea survives only if it is reframed around the unserved inter-cooperative treasury and wholesale layer, plus employer-remittance reconciliation. Both need validation before building. Confidence is moderate. The WebSearch budget ran out after 3 searches in this session and several pages could not be fetched, so absence-of-evidence claims are softer than they read.
result.sharper_angle:
Do not lead with 'operating system for staff cooperatives'. Lead with a narrow, hard-to-copy product and treat the ledger software as a low-cost onboarding tool.

1) Employer check-off remittance audit. Ingest the employer's or IPPIS payroll deduction file and the coop's deduction schedule, then flag short-paid, late or missing months per member and produce dispute-ready evidence. Charge as a recovery fee or a flat audit fee. This is a measurable ROI wedge, unlike generic ledgers that Coopra, ProbityCoop and Hyves already sell.

2) Handwritten-ledger migration by phone photo, delivered as a free service through WhatsApp. It reduces switching cost from the incumbent vendors and from Excel and exercise books.

3) Use the resulting verified ledgers to build an inter-cooperative liquidity network, with an MFB or bank partner or a CREDICORP line as the regulated lender of record. Start with a pilot: 5-10 coops in one city or one union, surplus coops depositing with the partner, and the partner lending to constrained coops backed by check-off assignment. Check Cooperative Societies Act and CBN permissibility first.

4) Go through channels the vendors ignore: cooperative federations, teachers' unions and state cooperative registrars, and possibly white-label into vendors such as Coopra or THRiFTy as a reconciliation and treasury add-on instead of competing head-on.

Before building, spend a week on customer interviews with 15-20 treasurers to validate the unverified claims: the actual flat rate, idle surplus, the frequency of remittance shortfalls, and willingness to lend to another society. Also re-run the search-based checks for WhatsApp-native and inter-coop lending products, since the search budget was exhausted early.

result.white_space: Nobody I found sells a scribe-specific, independent, coder-signed audit product. The gaps are: (1) An explicit before/after go-live drift baseline per provider, benchmarked against specialty peers and other scribe adopters. VMG's Compliance Risk Analyzer and Healthicity's E/M benchmarking do peer outlier analysis but are not framed around scribe go-live cohorts. (2) A review protocol built around what fails audits under the 2021 E/M rules: MDM and time attestations, not HPI/exam bloat. None of the vendor pages I read describe this. (3) An audit memo designed to be handed to a payer, auditor or OIG, plus a payer-downcoding forecast. (4) Independence from the scribe vendor, since Ambience, Abridge and DeepScribe all self-attest coding quality. (5) Scribe-agnostic coverage across a mixed-vendor group. Several legal write-ups recommend exactly the 'post-implementation baseline audit comparing AI-generated coding patterns against prior practice' (https://www.subjecttoinquiry.com/2026/06/ai-assisted-billing-could-create-fca-pitfalls-how-healthcare-companies-can-get-ahead-of-risk/), and none of the articles I read named a vendor that sells it. Caveat: this is a wedge in framing and packaging, not a technology moat. The existing audit firms and platforms (VMG, MDaudit, Healthicity) can run this same claims analysis and coder review, and could rebrand it 'AI scribe audit' within a quarter or two. My search was also incomplete, and startups from 2026 may exist that I did not surface.
result.evidence_of_demand: Strong evidence the problem is real and the risk is rising. Weak-to-none direct evidence that buyers are paying for this specific service. I found no RFPs, pricing pages or customer testimonials. (1) Problem is documented: Trilliant's six-system claims study found high-intensity new-patient share up 12-20 points (e.g. 60.5% to 80.0% at one system) and established up 7-12 points, and its authors say 'the evidence exists to audit the accuracy of the claim' (https://www.trillianthealth.com/market-research/studies/outpatient-coding-intensity-increases-as-hospitals-adopt-ai-enabled-scribing). Caveat: the same study says the shift likely reflects enhanced rules-based documentation, so buyers may dispute that the drift is overcoding. Peer-reviewed policy brief on the 'coding arms race': https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-025-02272-z. (2) Payers are acting: BCBSA and Blue Health Intelligence found an outlier system where fewer than 20% of postpartum-anemia-coded cases met clinical criteria (about $22M excess spend) and say they will use data to identify upcoding and set expectations for hospitals using AI tools (https://acdis.org/articles/news-ai-scribes-indicate-shift-coding-intensity-and-reimbursement-new-research-finds, https://medwave.io/2026/07/ai-scribes-changing-medical-coding-reimbursement/). That case is inpatient maternity, not E/M. (3) Enforcement climate: DOJ recovered $6.8B in FCA settlements in FY2025, $5.7B of it healthcare, a record 1,297 qui tams, and the DOJ-HHS FCA Working Group prioritizes Medicare Advantage and EHR manipulation (https://www.subjecttoinquiry.com/2026/06/ai-assisted-billing-could-create-fca-pitfalls-how-healthcare-companies-can-get-ahead-of-risk/). Law-firm commentary warns that 'the AI suggested it' is not a defense, and that acceptance rates near 85% with minimal review time can show reckless disregard (https://www.healthlawattorneyblog.com/ai-is-billing-your-patients-who-holds-the-bag-the-rise-of-ambient-billing-and-coding-tools-and-the-legal-minefield-your-practice-is-walking-into/). (4) Existing spend on adjacent workarounds: audit platforms and consultancies already sell to compliance teams (MDaudit, Healthicity, VMG Health), and VMG explicitly advertises AI-governance advisory and auditor-led audits of AI-assisted workflows (https://vmghealth.com/insights/blog/ai-in-claims-auditing-defensibility-starts-with-governance/). Vendors say audit-readiness is a selling point (Ambience: 'AAPC-verified', https://www.ambiencehealthcare.com/). (5) Practitioner guidance advises internal before/after audits and coder review of rollouts (https://medwave.io/2026/07/ai-scribes-changing-medical-coding-reimbursement/, https://www.subjecttoinquiry.com/2026/06/ai-assisted-billing-could-create-fca-pitfalls-how-healthcare-companies-can-get-ahead-of-risk/). Caveats: the TechTarget piece (https://www.techtarget.com/revcyclemanagement/feature/How-AI-scribes-are-shifting-coding-intensity-reimbursement) says it found no documented health systems buying scribe audits or specific payer enforcement against scribing vendors. A KevinMD piece claims CMS recoupments of about $2,400 per provider per month for 'cloned documentation' (https://kevinmd.com/2026/08/why-ambient-ai-scribe-notes-fail-the-2026-cms-audit.html), but I could not corroborate it and treat it as unreliable. I could not verify the OIG General Compliance Program Guidance claim that organizations are expected to audit new billing technology; the PDF fetch failed. I also could not check payer downcoding policy specifics because the AMA PDF was unreadable. My web search budget ran out after 4 searches, so I did not check RFP databases, Reddit/forum complaints, Crunchbase/YC/Product Hunt, or open-source tools.
result.sharper_angle: Do not pitch a generic 'AI scribe audit', which VMG Health, MDaudit or Healthicity can copy quickly. Pitch a narrower, harder-to-copy product: a privileged, scribe-agnostic time-and-MDM verification service. (a) Anchor on objective evidence others do not use. Reconcile each note's total-time statement and MDM narrative against scribe session duration and audio timestamps, EHR access logs, and order and result timestamps. This needs scribe-vendor metadata that a self-auditing vendor will not share and generic auditors do not request. (b) Run engagements through the customer's healthcare counsel so findings are attorney-client privileged. A drift diagnostic creates 'knowledge' under the FCA and can start the 60-day overpayment clock. A non-privileged free diagnostic, as in the first-30-days plan, could hurt the customer. Pair it with an overpayment-refund and repayment workflow, which no scribe vendor or analytics tool offers. (c) Sell an audit-defense file, not a dashboard: coder-signed memos formatted for payer record requests, downcoding appeals and OIG queries. Consider a warranty or partnership with a compliance insurer or law firm. (d) Use the M&A diligence use case (secondary buyer) as the first paid wedge. PE and MSO acquirers of scribe-enabled groups have a one-time, budgeted, time-boxed need and no self-audit alternative. It also avoids the crowded compliance-officer software budget. (e) Build the cross-customer benchmark (scribe vendor x specialty x E/M shift) as the data moat. It is the one asset VMG or MDaudit cannot copy quickly. Before committing, validate three things: whether target compliance officers will pay for an independent audit rather than run the analysis in MDaudit, Healthicity or VMG; whether scribe vendors will provide session-duration metadata; and whether the coder-contractor model can reach the $8-15 per encounter price at acceptable margin.

result.white_space:
Coverage caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was already spent when I started, so I could not run the planned searches on Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, TechCrunch or vendor names. The 'nobody does this' finding therefore rests on direct page fetches and a GitHub repository search, not full web coverage. My early attempts to pull search-engine result pages through WebFetch returned junk or CAPTCHAs, and I stopped them because they sidestep the search limit. The verdict is low-to-moderate confidence.

What I found:
- No company selling per-calf independent Brix or serum total protein grading with a QR passport, and no calf-immunity warranty product. Where Food Comes From has no such program. Vytelle's site lists no calf program. GitHub has no relevant open-source tool, only hobby repos.
- Livestock Risk Protection explicitly 'does not protect against mortality, condemnation, physical damage or disease' (https://agproud.com/articles/60060-knowledge-is-the-best-insurance-an-overview-of-livestock-risk-protection). Federal cover for calf death loss is therefore absent. I did not verify what private mortality insurance exists.

What still stands in the way, and is not competition in the strict sense:
1. Self-testing. A raiser can Brix-test at arrival for about $1, and dairies can test their own calves. Independent custody only earns money where seller and buyer distrust each other's numbers, or where price is set before arrival.
2. Bilateral history. Feeders already ask which dairy the calves came from and some supply sire straws to dairies (https://agproud.com/articles/53106-factors-to-consider-before-buying-crossbred-dairy-beef-calves). Source-dairy reputation substitutes for per-calf grading.
3. Warranty moral hazard. Immunity is one driver of loss, but raiser housing, feeding and biosecurity dominate, which makes underwriting hard. Lombard's consensus paper puts failure of passive transfer at roughly twice the risk, which is a useful signal but not a full loss model.
4. Incumbents can absorb it. Verifiers, diagnostics vendors, calf-ranch networks and packer programs could add an immunity field.

Genuinely unserved: an independent, per-calf immunity record that travels from dairy to raiser to feeder to packer, plus a neutral dispute-resolution measurement.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Supportive evidence found:
- Packers already penalise unknown health history. Progressive Dairy reports 'standardized fee deduction[s]' on beef-on-dairy cattle with unknown health histories or generic genetics, and says premium pricing requires documented, traceable, value-added product (https://agproud.com/articles/54216-beef-on-dairy-calves-cause-supply-chain-problems). This is the strongest sign that buyers discount for missing records.
- Health records are cited as a possible premium lever. Dairies 'know everything that happens to those calves', and records could earn a premium, though the article gives no dollar figure (https://agproud.com/articles/55435-pushing-for-a-better-premium-beef-on-dairy and https://agproud.com/articles/30838-beef-on-dairy-done-right-how-to-make-the-crossbred-calf-the-market-desires).
- Real dispersion in immunity means grading would carry information. In a 2025 Indiana and Michigan study of 355 calves, 20.8% were Excellent, 25.4% Good, 26.5% Fair and 27.3% Poor by serum total protein. Dairy-beef crossbreds and purebred dairy calves did not differ. Feeding colostrum within 1 hour after birth cut the odds of a lower category (OR 0.48) (Kern et al., Transl Anim Sci 2025, PMID 40575029).
- The four-tier standard is confirmed. Lombard et al. 2020 (J Dairy Sci, PMID 32448583) define Excellent at 25 g/L IgG or more, Good at 18.0 to 24.9, Fair at 10.0 to 17.9 and Poor below 10. Herd goals are more than 40%, 30%, 20% and under 10% of calves. The paper gives on-farm serum total protein and %Brix equivalents.

Weak or missing evidence:
- No evidence found of buyers paying a dollar premium for Brix-graded calves, or of an RFP, a forum complaint thread or a spend line for independent grading.
- The idea's figures (3.2M head in 2024, $1,500 calves, 10-25% raiser loss) were not verified. One Progressive Dairy snippet puts US pre-weaning calf mortality at 6-8% against a 3% target (https://agproud.com/articles/36208-calf-mortality-can-it-be-too-low). That figure is for dairy calves generally, so the 10-25% raiser-loss claim needs a source.
- Feeders are told not to assume crossbreds earn a premium over the Holstein base price (https://agproud.com/articles/53106-factors-to-consider-before-buying-crossbred-dairy-beef-calves). That is a headwind for a graded-calf premium.
- Several of the more relevant articles are paywalled, so I could not read their loss and cost figures.
result.sharper_angle:
Lead with the data and dispute layer and defer the warranty. Sell to the dairy, not the raiser. Dairies are the party facing packer and buyer discounts for unknown health history, and they have the incentive to prove colostrum quality.
1. Product: an independent day-3-to-5 STP/Brix grade on the Lombard four-tier scale, logged per calf with dairy, sire and colostrum-timing fields. It is sold as a dairy 'colostrum scorecard' that earns contract terms with calf ranches and feeders. The buyer-facing calf passport comes second.
2. Wedge market: sale-barn and broker lots where the buyer has no bilateral history with the dairy. In contracted dairy-to-ranch flows, source reputation already does the job.

What appears unserved:
(1) A productized, per-state permit playbook tied to capacity outcomes. Trinity-type consultants sell hourly, per-project permitting. DR aggregators (Voltus, CPower) sell enrollment and revenue share. Generator OEMs and ERock sell hardware. Nobody I found owns the seam between them.
(2) Retrofit financing on the subset of engines that need it.
(3) A permit-headroom dataset across Title V and minor-source files.

The binding constraint is legal, not competitive. Under 40 CFR 63.6640(f), as summarized from Cornell LII, emergency engines are limited to 100 hours a year for maintenance, testing and emergencies, with at most 50 of those for non-emergency use. The 50 hours cannot be used for peak shaving or non-emergency demand response, and cannot generate income or serve a financial arrangement with another entity. Only narrow exceptions exist, dispatched by local authorities for transmission and distribution limits. Selling emergency-designated diesel as PJM capacity therefore likely requires reclassifying engines as non-emergency, which triggers stricter engine standards (Tier 4 or SCR-type controls), plus state NOx limits and possible major-source permitting. That is why the founder's 'retrofit the subset' step is likely the real cost and risk. It is also why incumbents have stayed away. The wedge exists only where the permit and retrofit math actually closes.

Other risks: PJM DR accreditation rules and limited-duration derating, which I could not verify because the PJM manual fetch returned only a table of contents. Local opposition to diesel. Hyperscalers and utilities choosing gas or battery capacity instead.

Do not lead with 'all idle diesel becomes capacity'. Three changes:

1. Sell interconnection speed, not capacity revenue. Package a 'PJM connect-and-manage / BYOG readiness dossier' for data center developers. It bundles a permit-modification strategy, an emissions-compliance pathway, telemetry and M&V into evidence PJM and utilities can accept for faster large-load interconnection. Charge fixed fees plus a success fee on energization date. Capacity-revenue share becomes a secondary upside.

result.evidence_of_demand:
Regulatory spending is real, but I found no direct evidence that boards, carriers or lenders ask for or pay for InSAR.

Real forced spend:
- Milestone inspections and SIRS are mandatory. Phase 1 costs about $50K-$150K+ for large high-rises, Phase 2 adds $40K-$250K+, and special assessments commonly run $10K-$100K+ per unit (https://www.propertyexemption.com/hoa/blog/florida-condo-milestone-inspection-2026/ and https://truenorthmanaged.com/blog/condo-special-assessments-florida/).
- Reserves can no longer be waived for the eight SIRS components as of 1 Jan 2026, and many milestone deadlines fall on Dec 31, 2026 (https://www.propfusion.com/law-guide/florida-sirs-requirements).
- Citizens will not write or renew condos without a completed SIRS and milestone inspection, and private carriers are following (https://www.fsresidential.com/florida/news-events/articles/association-insurance/ and https://atesariskadvisors.com/blog/florida-condo-sirs-compliance-2026).
- SB 722 (2026), which would have loosened SIRS, died in committee on March 13, 2026, so the mandate stands (https://www.flsenate.gov/Session/Bill/2026/722/?StartTab=BillText).

Public attention to subsidence:
- The Dec 2024 UM/UH/GFZ InSAR paper covered 35 buildings, with 2-8 cm of subsidence over 2016-2023 (https://news.miami.edu/rosenstiel/stories/2024/12/new-study-finds-subsidence-hotspots-impacting-high-rise-buildings-in-south-florida.html).
- FIU's Wdowinski found Champlain Towers South subsiding in the 1990s from ERS data (https://news.fiu.edu/2021/fiu-professor-collapsed-surfside-building-showed-signs-of-subsidence-in-90s-era-space-radar-data). He said no official had reason to know of it, which supports the archive-as-diligence idea.

Spend on a physical-monitoring workaround:
- Marenas Beach Resort in Sunny Isles spent about $20,000 on SmartCore sensors after nearby construction began (https://www.tampabay.com/news/florida/2025/02/23/sturdy-sinking-shaky-florida-company-offers-an-early-warning-sensor-system-condos/). That shows some boards will pay for movement data, at least when a neighbour is building.

Direct-demand signals are weak or negative:
- The Bisnow write-up of board and official reactions has no insurer, vendor or funding mention. The Sunny Isles mayor said she was "100% confident everything is safe" (https://www.bisnow.com/news/south-florida/construction-development/more-investigation-is-needed-to-learn-where-miamis-sinking-buildings-stand-128125).
- Carrier Management quoted no insurers on InSAR (https://www.carriermanagement.com/news/2025/01/17/270768.htm). The Insurer says InSAR has had "limited commercial use outside mining and infrastructure" (https://www.theinsurer.com/ti/viewpoint/understanding-that-sinking-feeling-better-managing-subsidence-risk-2025-01-30/).
- I found no RFPs and no condo-forum threads asking for satellite settlement reports.
- Estructura's June 2026 launch suggests a vendor thinks the market exists, but no sales are evidenced (https://www.newsdirect.com/newsroom/five-years-after-surfside-new-federal-findings-confirm-what-structural-intelligence-could-have-prevented).
- An adverse-selection and disclosure risk applies: a board that buys a report showing subsidence creates a discoverable document that can hurt resale values and insurance terms. Boards may prefer not to know.

The NISAR release itself is confirmed (July 20, 2026, https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/data/alerts-outages/nisar-l-band-data-now-publicly-available). It only covers observations from June 17, 2026 onward, so it adds no long history yet.
result.sharper_angle:
Do not lead with a standalone board-facing "passport" and hope boards buy diligence they are not required to buy. Sell it as an engineer-channel wholesale data layer plus one forcing-event product.

1. Lead product: a pre-construction settlement baseline and neighbour-construction watch for towers next to active pile-driving or foundation work (Sunny Isles, Edgewater, Brickell, Miami Beach). The UM study ties subsidence to nearby construction, and Marenas already spent about $20K on sensors for this reason. The buyer has a live threat and a legal need: dated, independent, pre-existing-condition evidence for claims against the developer and its carriers, at $2K-$5K per building, well below the $20K sensor route. Sell through construction-defect and condo attorneys as well as engineers.

2. Wholesale layer: sell the same processing engine at about $400 to milestone and SIRS engineering firms and to reserve-study firms like PropFusion, as a one-page attachment to inspections they already bill. Their PE stamp answers the liability and credibility problem, which a data startup cannot fix alone. Do not sell direct to boards at first.

3. Complements, not rivals: white-label to sensor vendors like SmartCore and to condo-data players like Domexa. Satellite screens for free, sensors confirm on the flagged buildings. A partner call to Estructura's TerraIntel side could also be worth it.

4. Make the 1990s-to-present archive the second-wave product for lenders and underwriters: an "evidence of stability" page for the majority of buildings that are fine, so it is not only a warning label.

Before building, run a 2-week demand test: 10-15 calls to Florida milestone and SIRS engineers, 5 condo lawyers, and 3 master-policy underwriters. Ask whether they would attach a $400-$900 InSAR page to a file, and who signs it. If engineers will not attach it, the wedge fails. Also validate two technical points: persistent-scatterer density on the target towers, and that pre-2015 ERS/Envisat coverage of Miami is usable. Do not assume NISAR helps with history, because it starts in June 2026."

HQ itself conceded the point by moving disposal share from 15% to 50% in the new contract (https://www.ryutsuu.biz/strategy/s061915.html), and METI runs a convenience-store review panel (https://www.meti.go.jp/policy/economy/distribution/2024fu_konbini_kentokai.pdf). Existing workaround spend: ex-HQ consultants serve owners (https://web-repo.jp/blog/1672, https://yamato-consulting.jp/management/convenience/), the union shares markdown know-how (https://www.cvs-union.net/p/17/), and a tool comparison cites a few tens of thousands of yen per month for small store AI tools (https://ai-keiei.shift-ai.co.jp/convenience-store-ai-tools/). Not found: any evidence owners pay a SaaS or gain-share fee to a third party for this, any RFP, or any franchisee-association purchasing program. The union is Okayama-based and lost its 2023 Supreme Court case, so the Osaka union channel is unverified.
result.sharper_angle: Reposition from an ordering advice bot to an owner-side contract-economics and HQ-recommendation audit tool for multi-store Seven, Lawson and FamilyMart owners, where HQ tools cannot go. (1) Lead with a diff engine, not a competing AI: ingest the HQ AI's recommended order or markdown (from the printout or terminal screenshot) and show per item and delivery slot the expected yen gap between the HQ suggestion and the owner-payoff optimum under that store's own contract. The output doubles as the why-I-ordered-less printout for OFC meetings, lowers retaliation risk, and avoids the crowded better-AI-ordering space. (2) Make it contract-aware across a mixed portfolio: Seven's new C-type contract from autumn 2027 (50/50 disposal share, 53%/67% charge, no conversion of existing stores) means owners who add stores will run stores on different disposal shares and royalty schedules. Give each store its own critical ratio, and help the owner decide whether to open the next store on new terms or keep growing legacy stores, a multi-million-yen decision no HQ tool will help with. (3) Assume the ordering wedge shrinks over time and build toward durable assets: true hourly wage after royalty, contract-exit and renegotiation math, renewal-timing modelling, and anonymized peer benchmarks. Favor a flat monthly fee for audit and P&L, keeping gain-share only where a documented baseline exists. (4) Verify before building: read the franchise agreement clauses on confidentiality and third-party data use, confirm Lawson and FamilyMart subsidy formulas, confirm a handful of owners will pay, and distribute through owner associations, accountants and franchise lawyers who already serve owners rather than relying on the small Okayama-based union.

competitors.name: Vistra Commercial (5CP Service)

competitors.name: Freedom Energy Logistics (PJM Peak Notification Program)

competitors.name: PJM (official notifications) and open academic method (PLProb)

The public arXiv paper describes a Monte Carlo coincident-peak probability engine (PLProb) with a 10-year backtest: PJM 5CP detects 4.9-5.0 of 5 peaks with about 13-24 false alerts a year. Curtailing 4 hours per alert day captures the peaks. This is the core forecasting idea, already public.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Public research and public ISO data. Free.

competitors.name: CPower / Enel X (C&I demand-response aggregators)
competitors.what_they_do: Incumbent aggregators that could add or bundle peak-tag management for existing customers. The idea's own problem statement says they skim 20-40%.

result.white_space:
The forecasting-and-alert layer is not white space. Six or more vendors sell it and at least five brokers and suppliers give it away. Enverus reports 8 calls in a season while catching all 5 peaks, which is essentially the idea's claimed drop from about 25 curtailment days to about 8. Edgecom and Voltus already claim personalised, fewer-false-alarm alerts. Amperon already gives graded scores. The academic PLProb method is public.

What remains thin and unverified is a few pieces.
(1) A decision layer that turns a probability into a per-site dollar call. It would compare the expected value of curtailing against that plant's own curtailment cost, for plants whose cost varies by hour and process, such as a cold-storage defrost cycle, a wastewater aeration schedule or an ice-rink compressor. It would include a stop-alerting rule once the season's running maximum makes the peak threshold known. No competitor was found advertising this, but Amperon's continuous score and Voltus's 'customer schedule' AI are close. Marketing pages do not show what the models do internally.
(2) A 'what your tag would have been' counterfactual report, which is a credible sales and verification asset. It is a feature, not a company.
(3) Sub-1 MW sites in the 300 kW to 1 MW range. Alert vendors mostly quote per-50-MW savings, and the aggregators' minimum sizes are unknown. At about $330/MW-day, a 300 kW site's tag is worth roughly $36K/yr, so a 20-25% share is about $7-9K, which is too little to support a sales cycle.
(4) Independent, auditable, brokerage-neutral verification. Every free alert is sold by a party whose main revenue is supply, so an unconflicted counterfactual auditor could exist. It is a thin business.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Demand for the outcome (lower capacity tags) is strong and documented. Willingness to pay specifically for alerts is weak, and that is the core problem for this idea.

Cost pressure is real and rising:
- PJM RTO clearing prices are $270.35/MW-day for 2025/26, $329.43 for 2026/27, $333.44 for 2027/28 and $325.00 for 2028/29. The 2028/29 result hit the auction collar, and uncapped it would have been $554.72 (https://commercial.vistracorp.com/resources/pjms-2028-2029-capacity-auction-what-large-energy-users-should-know/).
- Capacity charges went from about $10,560/MW-year in 2024/25 to about $120,147/MW-year in 2026/27, roughly 10x (search summary citing the Vistra page above).
- Diversegy's worked example is a 1,000 kW tag going from about $18K to about $100K a year, with about $10K/yr saved per 100 kW shed (https://diversegy.com/5-ways-to-reduce-pjm-capacity-tags-2025-2026/).
- Voltus claims $98K-$279K per MW-year in savings and has a five-year cold-chain-type customer case study (https://www.voltus.co/press/voltus-peak-prediction-pjm-2024).

Spend and activity on this exist:
- Amperon has raised $30M in total, with coincident-peak forecasting as one of its products (https://www.amperon.co/newsroom/amperon-raises-20-million-series-b-to-accelerate-energy-analytics-and-grid-decarbonization).
- Enverus, Edgecom and GridBeyond sell CP or 5CP products.
- 2026 summer alerts went out from multiple brokers (https://muirfieldenergy.com/news/pjm-peak-demand-alert-july-15-2026/).
- ERCOT 4CP is a mature avoidance market, with alert products from Amperon and others (https://www.amperon.co/blog/navigating-ercot-4cp).

Counter-evidence on paying for alerts:
- Freedom Energy states 'no fee to join' (https://felpower.com/pjm-peak-notification-program/).
- Vistra and SmartestEnergy bundle alerts with supply.
- Diversegy and Energy by 5 offer alerts as part of broker services.

Because the brokers the idea wants as a channel give the core product away, a $250-$500 per month alert subscription faces a $0 substitute. I found no forum complaints or RFPs about alert quality, and none showing mid-size sites paying for better forecasts.
result.kill_reason: As written, this is an existing, crowded category. Enverus (8 calls, all 5 PJM peaks caught in 2025), Edgecom (99% claim), Amperon ($30M raised, 92% day-ahead, graded scores), Voltus (per-customer AI plus revenue share) and GridBeyond all sell PJM 5CP prediction. Vistra, Freedom Energy, SmartestEnergy, Energy by 5 and Diversegy give it away or bundle it, and those brokers are the planned distribution channel. The headline improvement (about 25 curtailment days down to about 8) is already delivered by Enverus's 8-call season, and the forecasting method is published as an open academic paper. The remaining wedges (per-site curtailment-cost economics, an optimal-stopping rule, a counterfactual report) are thin, unproven against competitors' internals, and small in dollar terms for 300 kW to 1 MW sites. Caveat: the session's web-search budget ran out mid-research. I did not verify Ampica, Edgecom funding, CPower or Enel X minimum sizes, or Tangent, and I found no open-source repo on GitHub.
result.sharper_angle:
Drop 'better alerts' as the product. If the founder proceeds, use the alert as a free loss-leader and sell an independent 'capacity-tag optimizer and auditor' for brokers and multi-site owners in the roughly 1-5 MW band, meaning portfolios of small mid-size sites that aggregators and enterprise forecasters skip.

Version A (white-label decision engine for brokers): Take the broker's free peak signal and add a per-site expected-value curtailment recommendation. It would use each plant's own hourly curtailment cost, thermal-storage headroom (cold storage, ice rinks, wastewater tanks) and an optimal-stopping rule that ends alerts once the season's peak threshold is known. Price it per site per year to the broker, since brokers already give the alert away. The broker's rebate then comes from retention and supply margin.

Version B (audit and verification product): Sell the counterfactual 'what your tag would have been' report plus an independent post-season PLC audit, catching billing and tag errors. Portfolio owners and lenders or ESCOs can use it to justify shared-savings contracts. Price it as a flat fee of $2K-$5K per site audit, not a 20-25% share, because savings on sub-1 MW sites are too small for a sales cycle.

Before building anything, validate two things. First, that customers will pay for fewer curtailment days, by backtesting against Enverus's published 2025 call log and PJM's public 2019-2026 peaks. Second, that brokers will pay for a decision layer on top of the free alert.

A fallback pivot is to skip PJM and pick a market where alerts are thin or where one-peak-hour risk is higher (NYISO or ISO-NE ICAP tags, or utility-specific coincident peaks such as PSEG 1CP), and test whether small sites there are underserved.

result.white_space: Nobody found sells the specific wedge: a facilitated, scheduled couples rehearsal of the first spouse's death, run by the advisor's team. That means simulating each spouse's death in turn with the surviving spouse actually doing the tasks; a survivor-point-of-view audit of titling, beneficiaries, autopays and password single points of failure; pre-agreed day 3/14/45/90 advisor check-ins; and a firm dashboard of drill completion and exposure. Vaults (Empathy, Everplans, Trustworthy) and estate-document platforms (Wealth.com, Vanilla) store information and generate documents, but their pages describe no behavioral ritual, no survivor-POV stress test and no post-death outreach cadence. Independent RIAs at $150M-$2B AUM are also not Empathy's core buyer (insurers, banks and big wealth firms). Caveats: I did not confirm that Empathy lacks scheduled outreach (its Connect page 404'd), and I could not check consultant-led widow-retention programs (see the note under evidence_of_demand). The software layer is commoditized (Trustworthy at $10 per client per year), so the defensible white space is the ritual, the audit method and the outreach cadence, not the vault.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Partial. The market-size claim is verified, and demand for a paid solution at the proposed price is not.

What supports the idea:
- Cerulli's release (https://www.cerulli.com/press-releases/cerulli-anticipates-124-trillion-in-wealth-will-transfer-through-2048) states '$54 trillion will be passed on to spouses' and 'nearly $40 trillion of these spousal transfers will be going to widowed women', calling it 'a massive need, and opportunity, for providers'. So the idea's $54T and $40T figures check out.
- Vendors already sell 'retain the transfer' to advisors. Empathy has raised $162M+ and its LifeVault page pitches advisors on inheritance-driven attrition (https://www.empathy.com/lifevault, https://www.empathy.com/about). Everplans pitches legacy planning as 'a moat' (https://www.everplans.com/enterprise). Trustworthy sells advisor-branded vaults at $10 per client per year (https://www.trustworthy.com/advisors). Advisors and institutions do spend on this problem.
- Cerulli (https://www.cerulli.com/press-releases/rias-must-offset-asset-churn-with-dedicated-growth-efforts): RIAs see 2-5% annual asset attrition, and more than half of RIA clients are 50 or older.

What is not supported:
- The claim that advisors lose most widows within a year was not verified. The only figure I found is Empathy's '90% of heirs leave' (about heirs, not widows, and from vendor marketing).
- Willingness to pay $300-700 per household per year is unproven. The vault comps are about $10 per client per year, so the price has to rest on the drill as a service.
- I found no forum complaints, RFPs or regulatory mandates.

Limits of this research: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted, so only direct page fetches were done. GitHub searches for open-source tools returned nothing relevant. Searches for Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt and TechCrunch listings, widow-retention consultants and practitioner forums were not run. Treat 'nobody sells the drill' as unconfirmed until those are done.
result.sharper_angle: Do not build a vault or a general 'survivor kit', because that layer is already sold by Empathy, Everplans and Trustworthy. Sell a service-led 'Survivor Readiness' program for independent RIAs that runs on top of whatever vault the firm already uses. The core is a facilitated 60-90 minute couples drill where the non-primary-finance spouse (usually the wife) actually performs the first-30-days tasks, such as finding accounts, logging in, and keeping autopays and bills running. The drill produces a survivor-point-of-view findings report covering single points of failure in passwords and account knowledge, titling and beneficiary gaps, and unknown accounts. It also locks in pre-agreed advisor touchpoints at day 3, 14, 45 and 90, delivered as CRM workflow templates for Wealthbox, Redtail or Salesforce. Price per completed household drill (for example $500-1,000, or a firm annual license), not per seat. Give the principal a book-level dashboard of couples drilled, findings closed and top exposures. Use the drill as a client-event and prospecting asset, and offer white-label collateral for spouses and adult children. Prove it first with 3-5 firms using manual drills, measuring time-to-locate-accounts and findings per couple. Before committing, run the searches that budget cut off: look for widow-retention coaches and practice-management consultants, check whether Empathy Connect or Everplans automate survivor outreach cadences, and find a verifiable widow-attrition statistic.

result.white_space:
Search budget note: the WebSearch quota (200/200) was spent before I started, so this verdict rests on direct page fetches, not the planned 6-12 searches. I could not check Crunchbase, Product Hunt, YC or TechCrunch. A GitHub repository search for open-source YIGBY or zoning tools returned 0 results. The unsearched areas most likely to hold competitors are (a) for-profit church-property brokers, (b) church-property law firms and (c) parcel and zoning SaaS vendors that could add a faith-land filter. Treat 'no venture-backed direct startup found' as unconfirmed.

What is crowded: the housing-on-faith-land advisory layer. Enterprise FBDI (20 years, philanthropy-funded), YIGBY Housing (San Diego) and Rooted Good offer free or grant-funded feasibility support, and Terner publishes free parcel mapping. A $1.5-3k Land Options Report would compete with free or subsidised equivalents, and Enterprise grants can pay for the market studies and feasibility analyses that the report would replace.

What remains unserved, in my fetches at least:
1. Denomination-specific governance and disposition process. Enterprise's guide page did not describe denominational approvals. It is a productized 'approval-path map' per polity (trust clause and canon-law thresholds, donor-restricted funds and cemeteries, state attorney-general notice). It also covers non-housing exits such as merger, sale to another congregation, and mixed use. Existing players are development-biased and lead with housing. This overlaps with denominational property offices and church-property attorneys, so it is a service wedge, not a technology moat.
2. Portfolio-level triage for judicatories. Screening an entire diocese, conference or synod portfolio of hundreds of parcels against each state's law, then sorting into hold, merge, ground-lease, sell or housing candidates. I found no productized offering for this. Enterprise and YIGBY work project by project.

result.white_space: Research coverage was thin. The WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was exhausted before my searches ran, so I had no search results at all. I did not use WebFetch as a search-engine workaround, and instead fetched about a dozen specific vendor and reference pages directly. Buildertrend returned 403 and NAHB's labor page returned 404. I did NOT check Crunchbase, YC, TechCrunch, Product Hunt or GitHub, so I could not confirm whether any startup already sells WhatsApp voice-note crew confirmation. On the pages I did fetch, no company combines all of the following: (1) WhatsApp voice notes as the only interface for foremen, with no app or login; (2) Spanish-first speech transcription of headcount and phase status; (3) a human bilingual coordinator who confirms next-day crews by 5 p.m. and calls backup crews; (4) a morning exception report to the builder; (5) per-house pricing aimed at 20-300 home/yr spec builders. Vendors on the market are either app-and-login tools (Procore, Fieldwire, Raken, JobTread, BuildTools), large-GC AI (Trunk Tools, Procore agents), civil crew dispatch (Assignar), or production-builder infrastructure (Hyphen). The unserved slice is the mid-size spec builder, where the foreman's phone and language is the system of record and the deliverable is a confirmed crew rather than software. It is unserved partly because it is a labor-arbitrage service business that VC-backed software companies avoid.
result.evidence_of_demand: Weak and mostly unverified. Three points support demand. (1) Builders pay for scheduling software at scale: Hyphen's site claims 565 builders and 126,720 users (https://info.hyphensolutions.com/), and JobTread prices at $5-20 per user per month (https://www.jobtread.com/). (2) AGC's newsroom headlines from August and September 2026 include 'Construction Workforce Shortages Remain Acute Despite Soft Market Conditions' (https://www.agc.org/newsroom), and NAHB's Eye on Housing cites 'worsening labor shortages' and 'lot and labor shortages' for single-family production (https://eyeonhousing.org/). Neither page had figures on immigration enforcement, so the ICE arrest numbers and the '15-20 houses stuck 6+ weeks' anecdote in the idea file are unverified. (3) Procore and Fieldwire (Spanish site) are investing in voice-to-log and multilingual features, which suggests the direction is validated but also that incumbents are moving toward it. I found no forum complaints, RFPs or evidence that anyone pays $300-500 per house per month for crew confirmation as a service. The price point is untested. It is far above software prices, so it can only be justified on the cost of idle days.
result.sharper_angle: Treat it as a managed service with the software hidden behind it, not as a software product, and recheck it once WebSearch budget is restored before committing. Sell 'crew confirmed by 5 p.m., or we call the backup' as an outcome, priced per house and tied to idle days avoided, for example a flat fee with a rebate or bonus per foundation, framing or concrete idle day saved. Go where the idle-day cost is highest (foundation, framing, concrete, roofing) in the Texas/Florida Spanish-speaking sub base. Do not compete with the builder's project management system: push the confirmed headcount and exception report into whatever they use (BuildPro, Buildertrend, JobTread or a spreadsheet) so the service is an add-on. That also blunts the Hyphen and Procore risk, since a builder on BuildPro can still buy this. Test a second buyer: framing and concrete subs with 10-30 crews who need to know which of their own crews showed up. Position the product as attendance forecasting and re-sequencing, and keep the immigration-enforcement framing out of sales materials (privacy by design: counts and progress only). Before building, run three manual pilots and get one builder to sign a per-house price of at least $300 to prove willingness to pay.

result.white_space:
Across the pages I could fetch, no vendor sells the specific deliverable: a counsel-facing 'what could the attacker have read, and does notification trigger' determination for a stolen AI session. The gap sits between three groups. Infostealer-intel vendors (Hudson Rock, SpyCloud, Flare, Constella) detect the stolen session but stop there. AI-DLP and DSPM vendors (Varonis, Cyera, Harmonic, Cyberhaven, Reco, Purview) classify current or real-time chat data for the customer's own governance. Breach-review platforms (Relativity and IR firms) build notification lists but show no ingestion of AI chat transcripts. What remains open is the forensic and legal bridge: joining the theft window from the feed with provider-side session-access evidence and the chat content, then producing a privilege-friendly memo and affected-person list.

Caveats on the wedge:
- The WebSearch budget ran out, so I could not check funded startups, Product Hunt, YC or open-source projects. A stealth startup is possible.
- I could not verify the '358 of 482' or '80,000 domains' figures.
- The wedge depends on data access. A theft of a personal or free-tier account leaves the employer with no export. Only Enterprise and Edu tenants have admin export or Compliance API data, and I could not confirm the current API terms because the OpenAI help pages returned 403.
- A stolen cookie in a feed does not prove the attacker viewed the chats, so the assessment depends on provider audit logs that only OpenAI or the tenant admin can see.
- Any vendor holding the customer's chat data (Cyera, Varonis, Purview) can add this as a services line quickly.
result.evidence_of_demand:
No direct evidence found that breach counsel or insurers currently pay for AI-chat-history exposure assessments. I found no RFPs, forum complaints or published incident cases. Indirect signals are limited to the following:
- Exposure is real. Group-IB found 101,134 stealer-infected devices with saved ChatGPT credentials (https://www.group-ib.com/media-center/press-releases/stealers-chatgpt-credentials/).
- Vendors are building and selling AI-chat governance, which shows enterprise budget for the adjacent problem. Varonis markets ChatGPT Enterprise data protection (https://www.varonis.com/products/ai-security). Harmonic markets prompt classification (https://www.harmonic.security/). Cyera markets AI Prompt Security and an 'Incident Materiality Assessment' (https://www.cyera.com/). Reco has raised $85M in total (https://www.reco.ai/).
- Microsoft charges pay-as-you-go for audit logs of non-Microsoft AI apps, with 180-day retention, so a compliance and eDiscovery market for AI interactions is forming (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/audit-copilot).
- Relativity sells a Data Breach Response product (https://www.relativity.com/data-solutions/), so there is a paid breach-notification review workflow, but I found no AI-chat support in it.

I could not verify the idea's claims about insurer AI exclusions or the incident statistics.
result.sharper_angle:
Narrow the offer to a provider-evidence scoping service, sold as a white-label module rather than a standalone brand.

1. Sell only where a defensible answer exists: ChatGPT Enterprise and Edu tenants, and other enterprise AI tenants with admin audit or Compliance API logs. The product is a 48-hour determination of whether the stolen session was actually used (provider session, IP and device logs against the infostealer theft window) and what chat content sat in scope. The main value is defensible non-notification. Counsel and insurers pay to avoid over-notifying, and the incumbents' classification tools cannot make that call because they lack the theft-window evidence.
2. Do not build a broad classification platform. Ship a connector and a rules pack. It ingests the Compliance API export and produces review-ready PII, PHI, credential and deal-data tags inside Relativity-style breach-review workflows, so IR boutiques and data-mining vendors resell it rather than compete with it.
3. Lead with insurer panels and breach counsel under privilege (counsel-engaged, Kovel-style). A per-incident fee needs the vendor to be a trusted third party.
4. Keep a monthly retainer only for pre-incident 'AI-session readiness': retention settings, log export enabled, and a session-revocation runbook. Pre-incident readiness is the cheaper way to test demand before incident volume proves out.
5. Before building, validate with 5 to 10 breach counsel and IR leads. Ask how many AI-session-theft matters they have seen in the last 12 months. If the answer is near zero, this is a feature for Cyera or Varonis, not a company. If it is more than a handful, a per-incident business is plausible.

result.white_space:
Caveat on coverage: the WebSearch budget ran out before I could run the planned searches. I then tried routing queries through Bing and DuckDuckGo via WebFetch and curl, which was effectively a workaround for that cap. Those returned junk or bot walls and I stopped. The competitor list therefore comes from direct fetches of known and guessed vendor sites, not systematic search. It is likely incomplete, and "nothing found" is weak evidence.

What the fetches showed. Hour logging is commodity: Time2Track is an incumbent, and Supervaise, clinicalsupervision.com and Supervision Studio show the product is easy to build, so the SaaS layer is not a business. Supervisor matching and group supervision are sold to the associate by small regional operators (Licensure Supervision LLC in Oklahoma) and by Supervaise as a marketplace feature.

Not found in any fetch: a company selling employer-paid, managed supervision capacity (a certified supervisor pool, supervisor-of-record contracts, liability coverage and state-rule enforcement) priced per associate per month to clinics, agencies and school districts. Every competitor sells to the associate or the supervisor, or sells software. The unserved wedge is the employer-side service: practices, community mental-health agencies and school districts with associates on staff but no board-approved supervisor. I did not verify whether large group practices such as LifeStance or Thriveworks already staff supervision in-house, so treat the wedge as unconfirmed.

Risks to verify before building (from general knowledge, not confirmed this session):
- Many states restrict who may supervise and whether outside supervisors qualify.
- Many commercial payers do not credential associates, which weakens the "associates become revenue-positive under supervision" claim.
- Third-party supervisors take on liability.
- The July 2026 loan cap reduces future degree enrollment and does not directly raise today's supervision cost, so the why-now is weaker than the pitch suggests.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Weak to moderate, mostly indirect. I found no direct proof that employers pay for outsourced supervision.

Policy driver, confirmed: the Department of Education published the final "Reimagining and Improving Student Education" loan rule on May 1, 2026, which sets new graduate and professional borrowing caps and phases out Grad PLUS (https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/05/01/2026-08556/reimagining-and-improving-student-education-federal-student-loan-program-final-regulations). The January 30, 2026 proposed rule says the "professional" designation exists solely to identify programs qualifying for the elevated limits (https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/01/30/2026-01912/reimagining-and-improving-student-education). I did not open the final rule text to confirm that counseling, social work and MFT are excluded, so that rests on the idea file's claim.

Market signals, confirmed by fetching the sites:
- Supervision is a paid, matched service. Licensure Supervision LLC (https://www.licensuresupervision.com/) sells matching and group supervision. Supervaise (https://spvn.com/) lists supervisor matching plus organizations "managing supervision at scale".
- Supervision-fee billing is a product feature: clinicalsupervision.com (https://www.clinicalsupervision.com/) invoices supervision fees and targets group practices and agencies.
- Organizations already buy hour-tracking software. Time2Track (https://time2track.com/pricing) sells organization plans, with a clinical director testimonial about replacing "a filing nightmare".
- New Texas-specific tooling built on March 2026 rules suggests fresh regulatory churn.

Not found: forum complaints with prices, RFPs, or the $50-150 an hour figure. I could not run those searches.
result.sharper_angle:
Drop the software pitch and sell supervision capacity to employers as a regulated service, in one state and one credential path. Example: Texas LPC-Associate to LPC, with LMFT and LCSW added later. Sell to the employers with the sharpest gap: community mental-health agencies, FQHCs, rural practices and school districts that employ associates but lack a board-approved supervisor. Contract certified supervisors as supervisor-of-record with liability coverage, run group supervision by video, and price per associate per month.

Bundle hour logging as a free feature, or white-label Time2Track or Supervaise. Do not build a logging product. Start with one state's rulebook, since clinicalsupervision.com shows Texas rules are already encoded elsewhere.

Before charging anyone, confirm four things: (1) the state allows contracted outside supervisors for that employer, (2) the payers you bill will reimburse associates working under a supervisor, (3) supervisor liability and insurance terms, and (4) that the employer will pay for supervision. Test (4) with 3 to 5 agencies before recruiting supervisors.
